title: Ashtpadi 5, salok: giving and taking
hookLine: the salok warns against clinging to gifts and forgetting the Giver

lines: A COIN ON AN OPEN PALM.
THE SAME COIN IN A FIST.
cards: Hold your hand out, palm up, a coin resting on it. Now close your fist around it. Tighter.
Your knuckles go white. Your whole arm is busy, and you can't pick anything else up, or wave, or shake a hand. Same coin, two ways of holding it.
Ashtpadi five of Sukhmani Sahib is about those two hands, and it opens with a short couplet, a salok, about what happens when the fist forgets who put the coin there.

teach.b: The salok has two lines. In the first, Guru Arjan names God denhaar, the Giver, literally the one whose nature is to give, and describes people who leave the Giver and attach themselves to other tastes, other pleasures.

Not bad things, necessarily: things that were given, now held as if they made themselves. The second line, signed Nanak, says such people never truly succeed, and that without the Name their honor slips away.
Notice what the salok doesn't say. It doesn't call the gifts wicked. The last ashtpadi named water, a breeze, family and hands among the gifts.

teach.h: THE GIFT CROWDS OUT THE GIVER.
teach.b: The trouble starts when the gift crowds out the Giver. A few stanzas later, the ashtpadi gives a picture for it.

teach.h: IN LOVE WITH A TREE'S SHADE.
teach.b: Someone falls in love with the shade of a tree. But shade moves with the sun. It passes, and he's left with regret in his mind.
The shade was real, and a gift. It just wasn't a possession. That line between giving and taking runs through this whole ashtpadi.
What comes from the Giver is received.
What's clung to as mine feels taken when it leaves. So the Sikh word here is not renouncing. Guru Arjan was a householder, and Sikhs are asked to live in the world.
The word is holding: open palm, not fist.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the start of the fifth ashtpadi; some readers take one ashtpadi a day, beginning with its salok.

o: the Giver, the one whose nature is to give
a debtor who must repay what he took
a beggar who receives what others give

games.q: the fifth salok — tap the pairs.
p: real, but it moves with the sun

s: the salok says good food and comfort are wicked
it warns against the gift crowding out the Giver, not against the gift.
the ashtpadi pictures someone in love with a tree's shade
the shade passes, and he's left with regret.
Sikh teaching asks people to leave home and renounce the world
Guru Arjan was a householder; the teaching is about how to hold, not whether to have.

games.q: you're resting in a tree's cool shade on a hot road. what do you do with it?
o: fence it off as your own.
enjoy it, glad, knowing it moves with the sun.
refuse to sit in it at all.
games.why: in the ashtpadi, the one who loves the shade as if it would last ends in regret; the shade was a gift, not a possession.

practice: Rest a small thing on your open palm, a phone, a ring, a key, and think where it came from.

Close your hand tightly around it for three breaths and feel the effort, then open it again and let it simply rest there as you breathe, the way someone sits in the shade, glad of it, not needing to own it.

wordCard.voice: Denhaar, the Giver: ashtpadi five opens with a salok about the Giver, and the people who keep the gift and forget the One who gave it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: denhaar, the Giver, the one whose nature is to give; the salok's name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: hold gifts loosely. Same coin, held in an open hand. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
